paragraphs: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday denied a Washington Post report that he is preparing a 2028 presidential bid, according to Fox News. The Post, citing three people briefed on his plans, reported that he was getting ready to seek the Republican nomination.

The newspaper reported that DeSantis had already contacted at least one national political consultant about working on a prospective campaign, and that a federal super PAC tied to him sent a fundraising text earlier this week.

DeSantis rejected the account on X. "The Washington Post is fabricating this out of whole cloth," he wrote. "I have not reached out to anybody about running for anything." When one user said they hoped the report was accurate, he replied that he was "sorry to disappoint." Asked about a suggestion that consultants might be using his name to draw attention, he wrote: "Probably the case. But maybe just made up by WaPo."

DeSantis ran for the 2024 Republican nomination, suspended his campaign in January 2024 after the Iowa caucuses and endorsed Donald Trump. He is term-limited and will leave office in January. Fox reports he has previously left open the possibility of another run.

The report comes days after midterm elections in which, per Fox, Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress. DeSantis said Wednesday it was "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans," noting that Florida would be the only one of the ten most populous states with Republican control of its government. Republican Byron Donalds won Florida's governor race. Fox said it had asked DeSantis' office and the Post for comment; no response was included.

The CDC has confirmed 5,182 measles cases in the United States so far in 2026, the highest number the agency has reported since 1991, according to data cited by Al Jazeera. The total is more than double the 2,289 cases confirmed in 2025.

Children and teenagers account for about 59 percent of cases: those under five make up 18 percent and those aged five to 19 make up 41 percent. Of the total, 4,993 cases were linked to outbreaks. Al Jazeera notes that kindergarten vaccination coverage fell from 95.2 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025-2026.

The CDC counts four measles deaths this year, fewer than state officials report. Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit state, reported six deaths and 1,487 cases. Governor Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr have been in dispute over how measles deaths are classified.

Pennsylvania counts "measles-associated" deaths when a person with confirmed measles dies within 30 days of developing symptoms, unless an unrelated event caused the death. In August the state reported two deaths of unvaccinated people. The CDC first included them in its tally, then removed them after Kennedy, whom Al Jazeera describes as a vaccine sceptic, questioned whether measles had caused or contributed to the deaths. Kennedy's own explanation was not in the article.

The CDC says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists on a standardized definition of measles deaths. Epidemiologists told Al Jazeera that tracking measles-associated deaths has long been a standard used by the World Health Organization and the CDC.

Voters rejected data center development in nearly every local ballot measure on the topic in Tuesday's midterms. Al Jazeera, citing the Data Centers on the Ballot project run by Redbud Consulting, reported 41 measures, with voters on track to reject development in all but one. CNBC, citing Ballotpedia and its own results, counted 41 measures across 10 states and said voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one.

The exception was Harwood, North Dakota, population under 800, where voters defeated a measure that would have required independent reviews of large industrial projects such as data centers. Two other contests were still being counted but were expected to favor rejecting or limiting data centers.

Experts told Al Jazeera the issue has become bipartisan and is tied to cost-of-living and job worries. A September poll found 70 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans supported limiting new construction. Tufts University's Bhaskar Chakravorti said voters were seeing the results "in their energy bills." A Dallas Fed working paper estimated data centers had raised wholesale electricity prices by 6.9 percent as of last year.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC on Friday that the company will keep investing, saying she does not think the election results dramatically changed anything. OpenAI published commitments Thursday for data centers it owns and operates. CNBC said the Nasdaq had its steepest drop in 19 months on Thursday, led by AI-linked shares, and rebounded somewhat Friday.
Al Jazeera says that with Democrats poised to control both chambers of Congress, the AI industry is likely to face more scrutiny from lawmakers.

Crusoe, a Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday that it sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google, TechCrunch reported. The company is eight years old.

Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe. Crusoe announced the project last year with Tallgrass, a Blackstone-backed infrastructure company, planning to scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity. Google did not disclose what it paid but announced plans to invest $17 billion in the campus.

TechCrunch says the deal highlights how hard it can be for independent developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Opposition from local communities can complicate development further.

Google and Crusoe are still working together: Crusoe is building another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas. Bloomberg first reported the Wyoming sale in June, and Crusoe raised a $3.9 billion round in September.

Crusoe's largest projects serve major AI names. Its Abilene, Texas, campus is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft is expected to open its first building in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that Jane Street signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal. Crusoe earns money by leasing space to customers who bring their own GPUs, renting out its own GPUs, and selling compute for running AI models.

Sequoia announced a broad overhaul this week in a memo posted to X that includes closing its London office and shutting down its scout program, TechCrunch reported. Scouts are select founders and operators who write checks on a firm's behalf, a model Sequoia pioneered 17 years ago.

Sequoia did not make a case against scouts in the memo. It framed the decision as a need for more focus, with a goal of "putting more energy behind fewer people and things." TechCrunch says observers warn against reading much into the London closure, given the city's thriving AI scene, while the scouts decision says more about where venture investing is headed.

Views on the model differ. Investor Sheel Mohnot wrote on X that it "never made sense to me," arguing scouts don't care much about the investments and firms can still miss deals, as Sequoia did with Uber. He suspected other firms will shut theirs too. Station F's Roxanne Varza, a Sequoia scout from 2020 to 2025, wrote that she was "sad" and hoped other funds won't follow. She said programs like it helped scouts build track records and relationships.

Andreessen Horowitz partner Gabriel Vasquez told TechCrunch earlier this year that the firm revamped its program: "They get more budget, but we have reduced the number." TechCrunch offers two reasons the model may have run its course: seasoned operators may earn more as angels investing their own money, and leading firms are now well known enough that the best founders tend to come to them.
TechCrunch says scout programs are more likely to be revamped than to disappear. Varza said venture partner-style deals are likely to continue, adding that Sequoia is "full of surprises."

President Donald Trump said at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, that NASA will launch the first nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars within the next two years, according to Fox News. "Within the next two years, NASA will launch the first-ever nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars," he said.

Trump described the mission as a step toward eventually sending American astronauts to the planet. "We're going to be paving the way for astronauts to plant the Stars and Stripes on the red planet," he said. Fox's report did not include technical details about the spacecraft. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman spoke before Trump and said, "We are going to venture farther into the solar system and move closer to that next giant leap." He described the administration's ultimate goal as the day American astronauts plant the flag on Mars.

Fox reported that the plan comes as NASA's Artemis program aims to establish a long-term human presence on the moon before eventually sending astronauts to Mars. Earlier this year, astronauts completed a lunar flyby during the Artemis II mission. Artemis III is scheduled to test spacecraft and landing systems in Earth orbit in 2027, and Artemis IV is expected to attempt a lunar landing in early 2028, before the end of Trump's presidential term.

Trump also said the United States "will establish a permanent presence on lunar soil." He pointed to the American Declaration of Freedom in Space, which he said he issued this week. Fox described it as asserting the right of Americans to explore and settle beyond Earth under U.S. law. Trump said it proclaims all of space open for American settlement. Fox also noted that the administration announced plans in August for a U.S. Space Academy to train students for careers in the Space Force, NASA and civilian spaceflight.

Haiti's National Police confirmed that a gang leader known as Mathias Saintil was "neutralised" during a recent law enforcement operation, according to Al Jazeera. In a social media post on Friday, officials described Saintil as the leader of the Boston gang, named for a neighbourhood in Cite Soleil, a poor part of the capital, Port-au-Prince. He was reportedly struck by multiple bullets, and a police source said he later died in hospital.
Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime wrote on social media, "One less gang leader. The battle to liberate the country from the grip of bandits continues with determination."

Al Jazeera reported that gang violence has surged for years, especially after the 2021 assassination of then-President Jovenel Moise. No national elections have been held since. According to the United Nations, as much as 90 percent of Port-au-Prince is under gang control and at least 26 gangs operate in and around the capital. The UN says at least 1.4 million people have been displaced, and 1,123 Haitians were killed between July and October.

An international Gang Suppression Force began arriving in April, and the UN Security Council extended its mandate until March 2027. Al Jazeera said the force has faced insufficient resources and staffing. On October 18, four Salvadoran aviation technicians involved in the force were kidnapped. El Salvador responded by sending as many as 2,000 troops, and President Nayib Bukele said the objective was to bring the four home alive.

Al Jazeera noted that human rights groups have criticised Bukele's heavy-handed approach to gangs in El Salvador. On Friday he asked a social media user for the exact address of a gang leader's house, saying, "we will destroy it."

The European Public Prosecutor's Office said on Friday that it carried out investigative measures at the headquarters of Spain's railway infrastructure manager Adif, the State Railway Safety Agency and Spain's Court of Auditors, according to Al Jazeera. The office said the steps follow an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds meant for upgrading safety, signaling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line.
Adif confirmed the visit to Reuters and said it complied and provided the information requested. The other two bodies did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

The probe follows an October 28 train collision in Urda, in Toledo province, which killed at least 69 passengers. It was the second fatal crash in Spain this year and led to the resignation of Transport Minister Oscar Puente, who called it a matter of political dignity. Adif president Luis Pedro Marco de la Pena quit the next day. Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo will fill the transport role until elections later this month, which Al Jazeera said could be affected by the tragedy.

The prosecutors had already opened a probe in March after a January crash in Adamuz that killed 46 people. That investigation looks at how EU funds for track maintenance were used, and there are no updates on it.

EU Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas called the closeness of the two accidents "very worrying." He said Spain asked the EU railway agency to help with its national investigation. Crash survivor Cristobal Gonzalez told Al Jazeera that more investment in safety is needed to stop further crashes.

CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Friday that next week's earnings from leading "neocloud" companies could test investor confidence in the battered data center trade. He spoke after stocks rebounded to end a turbulent election week in which, CNBC reported, investors dumped companies tied to the artificial intelligence build-out after Democrats flipped the House and Senate and some governorships.

Cramer called Friday's gains a "dead cat bounce" and said he sees plenty of sellers waiting for a bigger recovery so they can get out. He said concerns about data center spending and financing remain unresolved.

On the calendar, Constellation Energy reports before the bell, offering a look at how political uncertainty could affect power supply for data centers. CoreWeave reports after the close, and Cramer said the heavily indebted company needs to explain how it will finance expansion and manage borrowing costs. Nebius, another neocloud, also reports, and Cramer said investors want strong new orders, completed data centers and a robust project pipeline. "What I don't want to hear is that the sites they are building are coming in late and overbudget," he said.

Inflation is the other focus. The consumer price index arrives Tuesday morning, and Cramer is looking for a meaningful slowdown. He warned that persistently high prices could lead Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to raise rates again, after September's hike, the first in three years. The producer price index follows Friday.
Cramer also discussed reports from Cisco, Applied Materials, On Holding and Corteva, and a Kraft Heinz investor meeting on Thursday. He said he would pass on On Holding.

Ten years after the Paris climate agreement, its central goal of limiting warming to 1.5C has been missed, The Guardian reports. Temperatures have exceeded that threshold for two years, and the UN said weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate is now about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.

The Guardian describes the process as at an impasse. At last year's summit in Belem, Brazil's hosts removed national emissions-cutting plans from negotiation, calling them a matter for national governments. One developing-country negotiator told the paper there was "nothing to negotiate." The summit still ended with a deal, though the Guardian says few loved it.

The paper lists criticisms: the Paris rulebook took more than five years to agree, consensus rules let some countries obstruct progress, and the US has withdrawn under President Trump. It also says Australia, Turkey, the UK and Germany have fallen short, and most rich countries are cutting climate finance. Warming is now rising at 0.4C a decade, versus 0.2C in 2015.

Experts quoted still back the agreement. Johan Rockström of the Potsdam Institute said continued acceleration within the framework is a global failure, but also that "Paris is all we have." Former Panama climate envoy Juan Carlos Monterrey said, "Paris is our moral compass," adding that the speed of travel is not what it needs to be. Paul Bledsoe of American University suggested streamlining the structures to focus on national emissions goals.
This year's summit is the first with a split presidency and host: held in Turkey, presided over by Australia.

Stanford University researchers have implanted lab-grown human brain cells into mice engineered to lack much of their cerebral cortex, according to a study published in Nature and reported by Al Jazeera. The animals have been dubbed "alien-cortical mice."

The mice were genetically modified to be born without most of the cortex and the neighbouring hippocampus. When they were two days old, researchers injected human organoids, small lab-grown cell clusters made from healthy donors' stem cells. Overall, about 14 million mouse neurons were removed and about 4 million human ones added. The transplant worked in 25 of 29 mice.

Within three months the human tissue had grown about five times larger, connected to the blood supply and filled more than 90 percent of the cavities. The mice walked and vocalised mostly normally. In a maze test, mice without the implants kept getting lost while those with human cells did better. Some tissue developed into von Economo neurons, rare cells found in highly social animals. When exposed to low oxygen, the mice showed brain damage and poor limb coordination, which the researchers say may help study cerebral palsy.

Senior author Sergiu Pasca said the approach will not replace earlier models but gives access to aspects of human brain function otherwise hard to study. The researchers stressed the animals are not mice that think like humans, and stopped the experiments at six months, before any signs of consciousness appeared.

John Evans of the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved, said this experiment itself does not raise major ethical issues but could lead to ones that do. He suggested researchers not go beyond rodents for now.

Leaders of the Jehovah's Witnesses have relaxed the faith's ban on blood transfusions, the BBC reports, 23 days after the death of a follower who refused the treatment. Isaac Valdez, 26, of Waxahachie, Texas, had a seizure in a library in August and suffered a brain haemorrhage. He carried a "No Blood" card, and his family honoured his wishes when a neurosurgeon said the only way to save him was an operation requiring a transfusion. He died on 26 August when life support was turned off.

The Governing Body's change means most medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited, and individuals now decide. The rule dated to 1945. Spokesperson Paul Gillies told the BBC the change applies Bible principles to modern medicine. He said the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited, but components such as plasma, red blood cells and platelets are now allowed because the Bible does not mention them. The BBC says the change followed years of pressure from inside and outside the faith, which leaders do not cite as the reason.

Isaac's twin, Jacob Valdez, who had left the faith, told the BBC he believes Isaac could still be alive if the change had come sooner. He asked leaders for a straightforward apology. Gillies said families who have lost relatives "deserve to be heard compassionately." The BBC reported there was little clarity on why the change did not come earlier.
A 2016 medical journal study put the number of Witnesses dying each year after refusing blood at around 1,100, though the BBC says this is hard to determine among an estimated nine million followers.

Doctors in the UK removed a knife that had passed through a man's right eye and brain, and he recovered well, according to a case report published Friday in BMJ Case Report and summarized by Ars Technica. The man, in his 20s, arrived at hospital with the hilt protruding from his face. The 15 mm-wide blade had gone through the eye and brain, its tip hitting the top of his skull.

He was conscious and could talk and move all four limbs, but was confused and agitated. He scored 12 on the Glasgow Coma Scale, indicating a moderate brain injury. Doctors feared he might pull the knife out himself, so they sedated and intubated him, gave preventive treatment for infection including tetanus, and took images.

The scans showed the blade crossed the left frontal and temporal lobes, passing in front of the corpus callosum and missing the left internal capsule. It was close to the left internal carotid artery without apparently damaging it, though a branch of the middle cerebral artery looked indented.
Surgeons removed part of the skull and slid the blade out using a conservative method. They saw no significant bleeding. The right eye could not be saved and was removed.

The man recovered rapidly. His breathing tube came out a day later, and minor right-side weakness resolved in two days. He had no infections or seizures, and his language and coordination were preserved. How the injury happened is unclear, the doctors wrote, though they noted a history of depression. They concluded that outcomes may depend more on the precise trajectory than on apparent severity.

The Leonid meteor shower runs from now until 30 November, with its peak on the night of 17 November, the BBC reports. The report is aimed at UK viewers and says there could be up to 10 to 15 meteors per hour.

The shower is made up of dust particles from Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it travels around the Sun. The particles enter Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second, which the BBC says makes them the fastest meteors in the sky.

Experts advise finding a safe, dark spot away from light pollution, such as street lights. The meteors are visible to the naked eye, so binoculars or a telescope are not needed. Giving your eyes 20 to 30 minutes to adapt to the dark improves the chances of seeing them, and a wide open space gives the best view. Meteors could appear anywhere, but they seem to radiate from around the head of the constellation Leo, so that part of the sky is the best place to look.

The BBC says the weekend forecast is not ideal. Skies will often be dry but cloudy in many areas, with a chance of drizzle. The best chances of clear skies on Friday and Saturday nights appear to be in southern and western England and Wales, with more cloud farther north. By Sunday night, more of the UK is likely to be clear, although fog could form and temperatures could dip toward frost.
Viewing conditions look particularly good around the peak, because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight and its light is less likely to spoil the view.

President Donald Trump said the US military carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran on Friday, targeting an air defense system, and called the action "minor." He told reporters Iran had "built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five."

Iranian state media reported two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, the oil shipping route that has been disrupted since the US war on Iran began in February. State broadcaster IRIB also carried an Iranian army statement saying air defenses destroyed an American MQ-9 drone over the island. US Central Command told Al Jazeera the situation was "relatively calm" and declined further comment. The US had described "defensive" strikes on Monday near Qeshm, Hengam and Bandar Abbas.

Trump said talks with Tehran continue. "We've made a lot of progress with Iran," he said, without giving details. The Guardian reported that Iran's nuclear program remains the thorniest issue, and that Trump insists it be resolved in any deal. Late Friday, Central Command said the US was offering up to $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear program.

Qatar, which is mediating, said through its prime minister at Oxford that mediation continues to prevent the situation from spiraling and that the crisis "cannot be left unresolved." A Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al-Ansari, rejected reports that talks had failed. Qatar also said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke with his Qatari counterpart on Friday.

The strikes were the first since Tuesday's midterm elections. Both outlets report Trump has shifted between threatening to "destroy" Iran and suggesting a resolution is near. The New York Times, citing unnamed officials, reported US forces are poised to resume major combat if he orders it.

The US Treasury on Friday imposed sanctions on eight Canadian currency-exchange businesses it accuses of helping Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. The action is part of what the Treasury calls "Operation Economic Outcast."

According to the Treasury, the firms are based in Ontario and British Columbia and include Million Exchange, Amin Exchange and Cryptoyal. It said some also laundered proceeds by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets such as cryptocurrency, and that some helped an alleged head of a drug trafficking ring. The sanctions cut the firms off from the US dollar-based financial system, freeze any assets they hold in the US and bar transactions with American people or entities.

"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Canada's financial intelligence unit, FINTRAC, said it worked with the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, known as FinCEN, and that it can share intelligence with counterparts abroad through bilateral agreements.

In a separate action, FinCEN issued an order barring US financial institutions from processing fund transfers involving MEXC Global, which is incorporated in the Seychelles. FinCEN said the exchange has facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, among others.

The Treasury says its campaign aims to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Canada also lists as a terrorist organization. On Wednesday it sanctioned a network in India and Turkiye that it accuses of helping Iran evade limits on oil exports and airlines. The US claimed last week the campaign had pushed Iran's rial to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.

The US State Department's Rewards for Justice program is offering up to $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear program. In an announcement on X, it asked anyone with information on the program, its assets or associated individuals to send it through Signal or a Tor-based tip line. "You may be eligible for a reward and relocation," the program said.

The department said it is seeking information on nuclear scientists and staff, nuclear program-related technologies and capabilities, and associated organizations and personnel. It added that the US government "remains committed to countering any attempt by Iran to develop a nuclear weapons program."

Fox News reported that the announcement comes as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes on Iran while Washington and Tehran continue negotiating over the nuclear program. Trump repeated on Friday that Iran would never be permitted to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to earlier US operations against Iranian nuclear facilities.

According to Fox, Trump met his national security team on Thursday to consider resuming strikes, after he had promised to wait until after the midterm elections. Speaking in the Oval Office, he said Washington would "make a decision" on resuming the war. He asked whether the US wants to go further to ensure Iran's nuclear program is dead and "it will never happen again." He also said: "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You'll know soon enough."

Fox cited senior US officials as saying November 9 is a new moon in the Middle East, meaning little to no moonlight, a condition favorable for military operations. Reports citing a US official say Central Command is finalizing preparations for a possible resumption of major operations but has not received a new directive from Washington.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz, Ars Technica reports. It describes this as a possible sign that Iran is preparing to attack undersea infrastructure if the US and Israel renew strikes.

The maritime intelligence firm Windward tracked three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat near major cables in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables cross the strait, with two more partly under construction. Windward used ship-tracking data and satellite images and saw some vessels switch off their AIS transponders. It told the Financial Times the ships may be "mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark." Two of the tankers carried no commercial cargo and had no commercial reason to stop, Windward said in an October 26 blog post.

The stakes are high. Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar depend entirely on cables through the strait, and one third of India's westbound internet traffic passes through the Persian Gulf and the strait, the report says. One cable under construction, 2Africa, is owned by a consortium that includes Meta.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said in May it would "impose fees on Internet cables." More recently, Iranian officials and commanders have warned they could attack the cables directly. A Guard spokesperson said on October 20: "We remind the enemy of this."

The war has already affected the cables. Cable-laying ships have been unable to operate safely in the region, forcing 2Africa to pause its expansion, and US tech companies and Gulf countries are speeding work on routes that bypass the strait.

Russia launched a missile attack on Kyiv on Saturday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.

Klitschko wrote on Telegram that the enemy was hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles. He said debris struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district and damaged the facade of another residential building. The city's military administration said two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged. Officials continued to warn residents of possible further strikes.

The attack came three days before US-led talks between Ukraine and Russia were due to open in Abu Dhabi. The last such talks were held in February, and the war has gone on for more than four years. On Thursday, President Donald Trump said a deal may be imminent after meeting Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy of Russian President Vladimir Putin, at the White House. Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation that day.

Zelenskyy said in an interview aired Thursday that Kyiv is seeking specific guarantees from Western allies about how post-war security support would work. That followed two days of talks in Brussels on reconstruction, next year's funding and security guarantees, attended by officials from the US, UK, France, Germany and the EU, plus the World Bank and BlackRock, according to Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov.

A local truce in the southern city of Oleshky, which Melania Trump helped broker in October, expired last Sunday. The next day a Russian strike hit an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region. Ukraine's Emergency Service said Friday that the death toll had risen to 50.

New Zealand's governing centre-right National Party led early results in Saturday's general election with 31.19 percent of votes, ahead of the opposition centre-left Labour Party on 28.35 percent, according to Al Jazeera. The Electoral Commission said the centrist Opportunity Party will meet the 5 percent threshold to enter parliament.

Polling stations opened at 9am local time and closed at 7pm. The commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night. A final result, which will include ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27. There is no time frame for when a government must be formed.

The contest has come down to two men who share a first name. Christopher Luxon, 56, leads National and has been prime minister since 2023. A former chief executive of Air New Zealand, he entered parliament in 2020 and has emphasized his business credentials, according to The Guardian. Chris Hipkins, 48, leads Labour and is seeking a second stint as prime minister. He led the country for nine months after Jacinda Ardern resigned in January 2023, before Labour lost that year's election. The Guardian said some voters still associate him with Covid-19 lockdowns, while others respond to his pledges on healthcare and the cost of living.
On policy, National pledged to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme. Labour promised cheaper healthcare and transport.

New Zealand holds elections every three years under a mixed-member proportional system. Voters pick a local candidate and a party; electorate winners get seats, as do the highest-ranked members of each party based on its national vote, in a typically 120-seat parliament. All votes are counted by hand.

Paraguay's Congress impeached President Santiago Peña on Friday, and he was placed under house arrest minutes later, after the collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital lender with links to his business interests. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as interim president and, according to the BBC, will serve until 2028.

The Senate voted 44 to 0 to remove Peña, with one senator absent or abstaining depending on the outlet. The lower chamber had voted 78 to 0 to impeach him. Peña had offered to resign on Thursday, but lawmakers declined, which leaves him without the special jurisdiction former presidents enjoy. The BBC reported that charges alleged conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds and a cover-up involving the central bank. Peña denies wrongdoing, and his lawyer called the allegations a "reckless accusation."

Paraguay's central bank seized Ueno on Tuesday after saying it had fallen below legal solvency standards. About 2.9 million customers, around 60 percent of the country's adults according to The Guardian, lost access to their accounts, and protests spread, some with violent clashes. Reports put public and pension money invested in the bank between $355 million and about $860 million.

The Guardian reported that Peña held about $1 million in shares in the bank's parent company until April 2025 and appointed a former Ueno chief executive, Carlos Carvallo Spalding, to head the central bank. An arrest warrant was also issued for Carvallo. Peña said he bought the shares as an investor.
Prosecutors said Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday. Alliana said those affected "will be fully compensated." Al Jazeera reported at least 27 people face criminal charges in the scandal.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog says he will name on Sunday who gets the first attempt to form a government, after an inconclusive October 27 election left neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor former army chief Gadi Eisenkot with a majority.

In consultations that ended Thursday, 67 of 120 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot and 46 endorsed Netanyahu, Al Jazeera reported. Eisenkot's total depends on Arab-led parties, which won a record 19 seats and whom he has ruled out bringing into government. Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats, but United Torah Judaism withheld endorsement over the lack of an exemption from military service for ultra-Orthodox Israelis. Herzog has not committed to either man, citing "mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves."

The Joint List and Ra'am both backed Eisenkot. The Joint List said it would help from outside government and seeks guarantees including an end to house demolitions and action against crime. Ra'am says it is willing to join. Eisenkot has set conditions, including recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization. Netanyahu's Likud has said cooperating with Arab-led parties would be "dangerous to Israel." Israeli law allows a prime minister to take office with fewer than 61 seats if the government wins a confidence vote.

The Guardian reported that Tuesday's US midterm results, in which Democrats swept Congress, may push Israel's divided opposition to unite against Netanyahu, who has aligned himself closely with Trump. Opposition politician Yair Lapid urged rebuilding trust with the US, while Democrat Brad Lander said American voters want respect for international law and human rights.

The chosen nominee will have 28 days to form a coalition, extendable by 14. If that fails, a second nominee gets 28 days, and then a parliamentary majority can back a third candidate for a final 14 days.
